# Large multi-feature tasks

When a request is big — multiple features, or a large ask that naturally splits into independent
pieces of work — do not implement it as one monolithic pass. Split it into separate commits, one
per feature/unit of work, and drive each unit through this graph-engineering framework using the
Agent tool:

```
Task -> Planner -> Worker -> [Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2, ... Reviewer N] -> Synthesise -> Pass?
                     ^                                                        |
                     |-------------------- feedback (no) ---------------------|
                                                                               |
                                                                          (yes) -> commit -> next unit
```

- **Planner**: breaks the overall ask into an ordered list of commit-sized units of work (a
  Plan Reviewer can review the plan itself before execution starts; route its feedback back to
  the Planner and send a summary of plan feedback to the user).
- **Worker**: a resident agent (kept alive across the reviewer round for a given unit) that
  implements one unit of work.
- **Reviewers (1..N)**: spawn multiple reviewer agents in parallel against the Worker's output —
  e.g. correctness, simplification/efficiency, and test coverage as separate reviewer passes.
  These can be ephemeral (fresh agent per round).
- **Synthesise**: reconcile the reviewers' findings into one set of required changes.
- **Pass? gate**: if synthesised feedback has no blocking issues, finalize and commit that unit
  with its own commit message, then move to the next planned unit. If it fails, send the
  synthesised feedback back to the Worker as another round on the same unit (don't restart from
  the Planner unless the feedback reveals the plan itself was wrong).

Net effect: one commit per feature/unit, each vetted by multiple reviewer passes before it lands,
rather than a single large uncommitted or unreviewed diff at the end.

## Verifying UI work: visual recreation (the main way to verify)

For any unit that changes UI, the primary verification is a **visual recreation**: render the real
components with mock data and look at a screenshot. Typecheck and unit tests are necessary but do not
count as verifying how it looks. Workers should do this before reporting, and I re-do it (or open the
image for the user) when the user asks to see it.

1. Add a **temporary** preview route (e.g. `apps/web/app/zz-preview/page.tsx`) that imports the real
   components and renders them with realistic mock props: populated, empty, capped/failed, long
   names/links. Put context around them (page background, a mock frame for panels/drawers that need a
   session or client state) but never reimplement the component itself.
2. Start the dev server in the background with dummy env vars the app needs to boot (e.g.
   `CONVEX_URL=https://dummy.convex.cloud CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=x NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 bunx next dev -p <port>`),
   wait for "Ready", and `curl` the route for a 200.
3. Screenshot with headless Chrome, not the preview MCP tools (those time out):
   `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=2 --virtual-time-budget=6000 --window-size=<w>,<h> --screenshot=/tmp/<name>.png <url>`
   Take a wide desktop shot and a narrow one. Headless Chrome enforces a minimum window width, so a
   narrow shot can come out horizontally clipped; for true 320px checks render inside a 320px-wide
   iframe or measure element widths, and say so rather than treating clipping as a bug.
4. **Read the PNG** (the Read tool shows images) and actually look at it: hierarchy, spacing, truncation,
   overflow, alignment, tap targets, copy. Report what was seen versus what was not verified
   (hover/focus states, real clipboard/share, animations, Safari-only behavior, the real page behind auth).
5. For the user, `open` the desktop screenshot (copy it to `~/Downloads/<name>.png` first) since they
   can't see tool-output images.
6. **Clean up before committing**: stop the dev server (`pkill -f "next dev -p <port>"`), delete the
   preview route, temp public files and stray `.next` artifacts, and confirm `git status` shows only
   intended changes. Never commit a preview route or mocks.

# Mandatory visual + local-server verification (every agent, every run)

Applies to any task that changes code a user can see or that the running app depends on. No unit of
work is "done" until both of these have happened and been reported:

1. **Run it against the local server.** Start the real dev server (and `npx convex dev` when Convex
   code changed) in this worktree, wait for "Ready", and exercise the changed path end to end: `curl`
   the route for the expected status and hit changed API routes. A passing typecheck/lint/build alone
   does not count.
2. **Verify visually with a screenshot.** Follow the visual-recreation steps above (headless Chrome,
   wide + narrow shot), then Read the PNG and look at it. For pages behind auth, use a temporary
   preview route with mock data. Non-UI changes still get a screenshot of the affected page to prove
   nothing regressed.
3. **Report** what was seen, what was not verified (hover/focus, auth-gated pages, animations), and
   the screenshot path. If the server can't boot (e.g. missing env vars), say so explicitly and fix
   the env first (see below); never claim success without having run it.
4. Clean up (stop the server, delete preview routes/temp files) before committing.

Env vars: each worktree needs its own copy of the gitignored `.env*` files. If `.env.local` is
missing in the current worktree, symlink it from the canonical copy at `~/.config/avian/.env.local`
(`ln -s ~/.config/avian/.env.local .env.local`) before starting the server.

content.content: # AgentBisect `git bisect` for agent behavior. Give it a failing agent run (or just a known-good and known-bad commit). It finds the commit that broke the behavior, explains why that commit was written, and proves the culprit by reverting it. Built for neatHack (Oct 10, 2026). > Every figure below is copied from a file in `evidence/` (final re-run: [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md)). > Open the HTML reports with `open evidence/report-.html`; `evidence/dogfooding.md` covers using AgentBisect on its own build. ## What it is Agents regress in ways unit tests do not catch: a refactor changes the unit of a refund amount, a "helpful" change makes the agent cancel orders nobody asked to cancel, a new tool schema quietly doubles token spend. `git bisect` can find the commit, but it needs a deterministic good/bad test, and an LLM agent gives you a noisy one. AgentBisect supplies that test. It runs the target repo's eval suite at each commit it probes, in an isolated git worktree, with repeats and a calibrated baseline so a flaky run is not mistaken for a regression. Then it bisects. The demo target is [`support-agent-demo`](https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/support-agent-demo): a customer-support agent (pinned Haiku) with mocked tools, 24 eval cases at HEAD (18 exist at the good commit), and a seeded history of regressions written by a separate coding-agent session. ## How it works 1. **Intake.** Start from a neatlogs trace, a neatlogs detection, or a GitHub issue. Intake maps it to an eval case, finds a known-good commit (an earlier passing run of the same case), and records a `RegressionSpec`. 2. **Failure signatures.** At the bad end, every distinct failing check (for example `call_args:issue_refund.amount`, `must_not_call`, `budget:tokens@order_status`) becomes its own *signature*, and each is bisected separately. One range can hide several regressions; bisecting "the suite fails" would blame whichever commit lands last. A signature that also fails at the good end is a known pre-existing failure, and AgentBisect refuses to bisect it instead of inventing a culprit. 3. **Plain bisect.** Classic binary search over `git rev-list --first-parent`, with a monotonic probe after convergence that flags "multiple regressions likely" when the history is not clean good-then-bad. 4. **Smart (weighted) bisect.** A planner ranks the commits in range by how likely each is to be the culprit, then picks the next commit by weighted bisection (split the probability mass, not the commit count) and falls back to plain when the ranking is uninformative. Signals, in order: - **Span divergence**: where the bad run first differs from a good run (a different tool, different arguments, an extra step). See [span divergence](#span-divergence-and-the-fixture-fallback). - **Code impact**: `entire graph impact` finds which commits touched the code behind the divergent tool. - **Entire intent**: each candidate's [Entire](https://entire.io) checkpoint (the prompt and reasoning of the coding session that wrote it). Commits that were *meant* to change the failing area rank higher. 5. **Median budget checks.** Token and step regressions are judged against a per-case **median** from a one-time calibration run at the good commit (`agentbisect calibrate`), never recalibrated mid-investigation. A run is over budget past 1.5x the case median. Medians, not means, so one slow sample does not move the line. 6. **Verifier (revert test).** The culprit is only reported with confidence if reverting it at the bad end flips the signature from failing to passing (before and after pass rates are recorded). Revert conflicts, partial reverts and unbuildable trees lower confidence or end as `inconclusive`. 7. **Explain.** The culprit report quotes the Entire checkpoint (why the commit was written), the semantic diff, and the first span divergence, so the answer is "this commit, written to do X, causes Y", not just a SHA. 8. **Fixer (upcoming).** A fresh agent that sees only the culprit diff, the stated intent, and the failing evidence (never the planted-regression metadata) proposes a fix that keeps the intent. **Not built yet.** `report --open-pr` is a dry run by default and needs `--confirm-open-pr` to push anything. Roles, model pins and isolation rules are in [`ROLES.md`](ROLES.md). The agent and judge models are pinned and recorded in every result, and results produced under different pins are never mixed. ### Measured so far | What | Result | Source | |---|---|---| | Planner context with the Entire graph vs reading the raw range | 12,869 vs 26,420 tokens (51.3% cut). Measured on investigation `6857f0b738`, a different range from the final re-run | [`evidence/entire-context-savings.md`](evidence/entire-context-savings.md) | | Signatures correct on the full-range re-run (good `1b40b27`, bad `0ecffc0`) | 4 of 6 | [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md) | | Revert tests | 2 passed, 2 failed, 1 inconclusive; the sixth signature (es2) was correctly refused as a pre-existing failure, so none was run | same | | Eval rounds, plain vs smart | 24 vs 18, 4 vs 3, 84 vs 96, 54 vs 60, 21 vs 21. Smart won on the two behavioural signatures and lost on budget signatures (84 vs 96, 54 vs 60), tied on one (21 vs 21) | same | `agentbisect summary --format md` regenerates the per-signature table from saved state. ## Setup Requirements: Python 3.11 to 3.13 (the neatlogs SDK does not support 3.14), [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), `git`, and for the full pipeline the `entire` CLI with the `graph` plugin. ```bash uv sync cp .env.example .env # NEATLOGS_API_KEY, NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID, ... uv run pytest -q # fake executors and throwaway git repos; no model or network calls ``` The target repo needs `evals/cases.jsonl` and the eval CLI contract (`python -m evals run --json --isolate ...`, schema version 1) described in the `support-agent-demo` repo. Clone it next to this one. Optional pieces: - **neatlogs CLI** (`npm i -g --prefix ~/.local/neatlogs-cli neatlogs-cli`) for live trace intake, after a one-time `auth login --device`. See `hackathon.md`. - **Entire** (`entire enable` in the target repo; `entire plugin install graph`) for checkpoint intent and code impact. Without it the planner falls back to commit messages and plain bisect. - **LLM backend.** Either set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or run on your own logged-in `claude` CLI with `--llm-proxy auto` (personal use, your own login only; see `ROLES.md`). The proxy cannot set temperature, so repeats absorb the extra noise. ## Usage ```bash # 1. Calibrate the token baseline once, at the known-good commit uv run agentbisect calibrate --repo ../support-agent-demo --good 1b40b27 --llm-proxy auto # 2. Investigate from a bad trace (or --detection ID, or --issue URL) uv run agentbisect investigate --trace --repo ../support-agent-demo \ --strategy smart --all-signatures --all-categories --llm-proxy auto # or skip neatlogs and name the range yourself uv run agentbisect investigate --trace --repo ../support-agent-demo \ --fixtures path/to/bundle.json --good 1b40b27 --bad 0ecffc0 uv run agentbisect status [ID] # investigations and their steps uv run agentbisect resume ID # continue after an interruption uv run agentbisect compare ID # plain vs smart: eval rounds and cost uv run agentbisect summary --format md # per-signature results table uv run agentbisect report ID # Markdown + HTML report in evidence/ ``` State lives in `.agentbisect/` (atomic writes, resumable mid-step). Run `uv run agentbisect --help` for all flags. ### Span divergence and the fixture fallback Live span divergence reads multi-span traces from neatlogs. At the time of writing, those traces finalize as `dlq` with zero spans (see Limitations), so for the demo the same step runs on a **recorded fixture**: ```bash uv run python -m agentbisect.fixtures fixtures/divergence/os1-search-help ``` ``` FIXTURE: recorded from real eval-runner output (tool calls of one case at a good and a bad commit). Not live neatlogs data. good local-3b41... (1b40b27...), bad local-5455... (0ecffc0...), case os1 first divergence: step 1: bad run made an extra step search_help ``` The fixture is the tool-call sequence of case `os1` ("Where is order 1042?") at `1b40b27` and `0ecffc0`, taken from real `python -m evals run --json` output (Haiku through the llm-proxy). It is always labelled as a fixture, never presented as live neatlogs data. The bad commit is the tip of the range, so the fixture shows where behavior changed (an extra `search_help` step), not which commit caused it. ## boardui
BoardUI is a React + Tailwind CSS v4 design system (Next.js first) with free components and paid Pro components/templates. This server installs component source directly into the user's project — no terminal needed.

Typical flow:
1. In a project without BoardUI, call init_boardui once (installs Tailwind v4 + runtime deps, writes styles/ and utils/).
2. Discover with list_components; read source/props with get_component; get working code with get_usage_examples.
3. Install with install_components — it writes the files and installs npm deps.

Component names are exact — when unsure, call list_components instead of guessing.

## RTL Support

BoardUI supports Arabic, Hebrew, and other right-to-left languages across free components, Pro blocks, and templates. The same source handles RTL and LTR; there is no RTL CLI flag or separate component version.

1. Read get_component and get_usage_examples for the free `direction` item. Install it with install_components (stdio), or write its source and dependencies yourself (read-only HTTP). CLI equivalent: `npx boardui@latest add direction`.
2. Wrap the app with DirectionProvider using an explicit BCP 47 locale: `ar` for Arabic, `he` for Hebrew, `en-US` for English. Set matching `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` for a full-app RTL layout. CSS dir alone does not configure React Aria keyboard navigation, calendars, or portalled menus.

```tsx
import { DirectionProvider } from "@/components/foundations/direction/direction";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
      <body>
        <DirectionProvider locale="ar">{children}</DirectionProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

3. Use logical styles such as ps/pe, ms/me, start/end, and text-start/text-end. Mirror navigation arrows and drawer motion; preserve physical coordinates for charts, canvas, and decorative art. Custom portals should carry `dir={useDirection()}` on their root. Nest DirectionProvider for mixed-language regions.
4. Keep email addresses, URLs, OTP digits, and code LTR; isolate mixed text with bdi or dir=auto. Choose fonts with Arabic or Hebrew coverage and avoid extra letter spacing for Arabic. Translate application labels and accessible names in the application's translation layer; use Intl for dates, numbers, and currencies. Optional `template-copy` supplies TemplateCopyProvider for translating template display copy. Chinese (`zh-CN`) remains LTR.
5. For older installations, refresh the provider, component source, shared dependencies, and global styles. Preserve customizations before using overwrite. Pro updates use the licensed CLI or updated source downloads.

Setup and live Arabic/Hebrew examples: https://www.boardui.com/rtl

w,i=sys.argv[1:3]; p=f"{w}/state/investigations/{i}.json"
